subject: Biology
title: What Are Bacteria?
description: A micro-lesson that makes What Are Bacteria? usable.

hook.text: Bacteria are single-celled organisms with no nucleus. They were the first life on Earth.

buildup.text: A typical bacterium is about one micrometer long—a thousand times smaller than a grain of sand.

discovery.text: They come in three main shapes: spheres, rods, and spirals.

twist.text: Bacteria reproduce by splitting in two. Under ideal conditions, one becomes a billion in 10 hours.

climax.text: There are more bacteria in your gut than human cells in your entire body.

punchline.text: Simple, ancient, and everywhere you look.

details.summary: Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotic organisms lacking a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. They are among Earth's most ancient and abundant life forms, reproducing by binary fission and thriving in virtually every environment from ocean trenches to human intestines.
details.whyItMatters: Bacteria are the foundation of Earth's biosphere, driving nutrient cycles and decomposition essential for all life. Understanding bacterial biology is fundamental to medicine, agriculture, biotechnology, and environmental science.
takeaways: Bacteria lack a nucleus, keeping their circular DNA free in the cytoplasm
Binary fission allows bacteria to double in number every 20 minutes under ideal conditions
Bacteria were the only life on Earth for roughly 2 billion years

faq.question: What makes bacteria different from human cells?
faq.answer: Bacteria lack a nucleus, mitochondria, and other membrane-bound organelles. They have circular DNA rather than linear chromosomes. Their cell walls contain peptidoglycan absent in animal cells. These differences allow antibiotics to target bacteria without harming human cells.

faq.question: How small are bacteria?
faq.answer: Most bacteria measure 0.5 to 5 micrometers, roughly 10 times smaller than human cells. About 1,000 could fit across a single millimeter. Despite their tiny size, a human body contains trillions of bacteria, roughly equal to the number of human cells.
